title: The One-Word Census: Answer-Choice Conformity Across 44 Language Models

model.params_source: paper Sec. 3.1 ('max_tokens is 1024 and requested temperature is 1.0 for every model'); top_p assumed

task.subset_rule: all 31 frozen stimuli (Sec. 3.1), each asked four times (Sec. 3.5, 'Each model was queried four times per prompt') = 124 calls per seed
task.approximation: The paper served every model through OpenRouter under the alias 'gpt-4-turbo' in July 2026; this run calls the dated snapshot gpt-4-turbo-2024-04-09 on the OpenAI API directly, so routing and any provider-side sampling differences are not reproduced. Self-distinctness is a within-model statistic, so it does not depend on the other 43 models; the plural merge, which the authors apply over the whole panel's answers for a category, is applied here to our own four answers only.

items.source: Sec. 3.1 of the paper (the 31 prompts are printed in full); identical to spec/stimulus.json of https://github.com/tap2k/modelun/tree/main/studies/consensus, which the paper names as the frozen stimulus
items.license: repository is public (Data and code availability section); the stimuli are the paper's own text

items.hook: harness/tierb/hooks/W7169474262.py (expands each stimulus to four runs, applies the authors' normalizer and computes self-distinctness)

fields_paper.label: the category id, used only to group the four runs

prompt.source_location: Sec. 3.1 'Stimulus' (30 category prompts of the form 'Name a[n] X. Reply with one word only.' plus 'Pick a word. Reply with one word only.'); no system prompt, fresh single-turn conversation each time
prompt.verbatim: full: the 31 prompts are given verbatim in items.inline. Sec. 3.1 prints the template with the placeholder article 'a[n]' and the 30 category names; the resolved wording of each prompt (including 'Name an herb.' and 'Name a musical instrument.') is taken from spec/stimulus.json in the repository the paper points to, which the paper calls the frozen stimulus.

output.postprocess: hook parse: the authors' norm() (analyze.py) - junk guard first (chat-template artifacts, replies over 15 words, bare acknowledgments -> failed cell), then lowercase, punctuation and emoji stripped, last alphabetic word kept, single-letter tokens dropped

metric.name: custom
metric.definition: self-distinctness: for each category, the number of distinct normalized answers divided by the number of valid samples (4 unless a cell failed); the score is the mean over the 31 categories. Bare plurals are merged with their singulars inside a category pool.
metric.original_location: Table 1 (appendix scorecard), rank 10, row 'gpt-4-turbo': 2.05 [1.67, 2.45] surprisal, 51% modal avoidance, 1% novel, 40% self-distinctness
metric.bootstrap_unit: category (set-level statistic: the runner resamples items and recomputes the mean)

cost.cost_note: the dry-run charges max_tokens as output; the real replies are one word, so the true cost is near the paper's stated ~$1 per model.
cost.prepare_note: runner --prepare --dry-run 2026-09-19: 124 items x 3 seeds, $4.53 (the battery's own dry-run line says $11.50 because it charges the full max_tokens of 1024 as output)

open_points: The headline metric of the paper (answer-choice surprisal) is leave-one-out against the other 43 models and cannot be recomputed from a single model's answers; self-distinctness is the cell chosen here because it is defined within a model. If the surprisal row is wanted instead, the panel's transcripts in the repository would have to be used as the field, which is a different comparison (our answers scored against their 2026 field).

Requested temperature 1.0 is part of the paper's design and is not honored uniformly by providers (the paper's own caveat); three seeds of four runs each give some grip on how much of the 40% is sampling spread.
notes: Four runs per prompt are the paper's protocol, so they are items (124 rows = 31 categories x 4 runs) and the harness's three seeds sit on top: each seed yields one complete replication of the paper's measurement. The repository also ships analyze.py, from which parse() and score() are transcribed.
